name: PAPA syndrome
aliases: pyogenic arthritis, pyoderma gangrenosum and acne syndrome

reference.source: Textbook of Autoinflammation / Rook's Textbook of Dermatology
clinicalPearls: An autosomal dominant autoinflammatory disease caused by mutations in PSTPIP1, which regulates the pyrin inflammasome
Classic triad is recurrent sterile pyogenic arthritis, pyoderma gangrenosum, and severe cystic acne
Joint disease often begins in childhood with recurrent, destructive, sterile arthritis triggered by minor trauma
Pyoderma gangrenosum and severe nodulocystic acne tend to become more prominent from adolescence
Aspirated joint fluid is sterile and neutrophil-rich, reflecting an autoinflammatory rather than infective arthritis
Interleukin-1 and tumour necrosis factor directed biologics are the main therapies, with variable individual response
The skin lesions can pathergically worsen after surgery or trauma, so aggressive surgical debridement should be approached cautiously
reference.pathophysiology: PAPA syndrome arises from dominant mutations in PSTPIP1 (also called CD2 binding protein 1), a protein that interacts with pyrin to regulate inflammasome activity. Mutations enhance PSTPIP1 binding to pyrin, promoting inappropriate inflammasome assembly and excess interleukin-1 beta production. The resulting sterile neutrophilic inflammation targets joints, skin, and pilosebaceous units, producing pyogenic arthritis, pyoderma gangrenosum, and cystic acne. Because both interleukin-1 and tumour necrosis factor contribute to the inflammation, biologics against these cytokines are used therapeutically.
additionalDifferentials: Severe nodulocystic acne without systemic disease
additionalInvestigations: Synovial fluid analysis and culture demonstrating sterile neutrophilic arthritis
Skin biopsy of pyoderma gangrenosum lesions
Joint imaging to assess destructive arthritis
Wound swabs to exclude secondary infection of skin ulcers
redFlags: Rapidly progressive destructive arthritis threatening joint integrity
Enlarging pyoderma gangrenosum ulcers with secondary infection
Pathergy with wound breakdown after surgery or trauma
Systemic inflammatory response requiring escalation of therapy
reference.prognosis: PAPA syndrome is a chronic relapsing disease; biologic therapy can control inflammation and limit joint and skin damage, but responses vary and established joint destruction or skin scarring may persist.
pitfalls: Treating sterile pyogenic arthritis as septic and pursuing repeated invasive intervention
Aggressively debriding pyoderma gangrenosum, which can provoke pathergy and worsen ulcers
Assuming acne is cosmetic and missing the wider autoinflammatory diagnosis
Not testing for PSTPIP1 in a child with recurrent sterile arthritis and skin disease
management: Interleukin-1 blockade with anakinra or canakinumab as key targeted therapy for the sterile pyogenic arthritis and skin inflammation
Tumour necrosis factor inhibitors such as etanercept, infliximab or adalimumab as an alternative or adjunctive biologic
Corticosteroids, systemic and intra-articular, for acute flares of pyogenic arthritis
Dedicated management of pyoderma gangrenosum with topical and systemic immunosuppression and careful wound care, avoiding aggressive debridement because of pathergy
Treatment of severe nodulocystic acne with topical and systemic agents including oral retinoids
Confirm sterility with joint fluid and wound cultures to avoid unnecessary antibiotics and distinguish from infection
Genetic counselling for autosomal dominant PSTPIP1 inheritance
Multidisciplinary care across rheumatology, dermatology and clinical immunology
